Ignominious

ig-nuh-MIN-ee-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Ignominious is humiliating or deeply embarrassing, often describing a public defeat or failure.

The once-favored team suffered an ignominious loss to a school one-tenth its size.

Worked Example

His ignominious exit from the company -- escorted out by security in front of his own team -- became office legend.

Ignominious describes a defeat, failure, or exit so humiliating it becomes publicly memorable.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

humiliating: Humiliating means causing a painful loss of dignity, and it can happen anywhere -- even in private, with only one witness. Ignominious is larger and more public: a defeat, exit, or failure so humiliating that everyone sees it and remembers it.

shameful: Shameful describes something that deserves real blame because it was wrong to do. An ignominious defeat may involve no wrongdoing at all -- a team can simply collapse -- while a shameful act breaks a moral rule people expected you to keep.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

triumphant: having won a victory; celebrating success

glorious: having or bringing great honor or admiration

Where it sits · how deep the shame cuts — embarrassing → ignominious → disgraceful

embarrassing vs. ignominious: Embarrassing is a mild, everyday word for discomfort; ignominious describes a much deeper, public humiliation.

disgraceful vs. ignominious: Disgraceful goes further than ignominious, adding a stronger moral judgment that the outcome brought shame, not just embarrassment.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ig-

prefix — ig-: not (Latin (in-))

root — nomin

root — nomin: name (Latin (nomen))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: full of, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: ig- ('not') + nomin ('name') + -ious together trace back to 'without a good name' -- exactly the disgrace ignominious describes.

Use the root in a new word: nominate

Use the root in a new word: nominate: Nominate shares the same Latin root nomen ('name'), literally meaning to put someone's name forward.
